EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal storm passed south of southern New England on Saturday with an inverted trough extending NW over the region. This led to widespread 3-5 inches of snow in central and eastern MA, eastern CT, and RI. However, there were two heavy bands that set up over northeast MA and eastern CT/RI which dropped narrow swaths of 9-13 inches of snow. Impacts were more limited because it was a weekend.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island. In Connecticut winds were generally lighter and not damaging with snowfall amounts in the 8 to 20 inch range. The highest amounts in Connecticut were in the eastern part of the state. Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 9 to 12 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest reports included 17 inches in Marlborough and 16.5 inches in Burlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck northwest Connecticut on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast. ||Confidence increased sufficiently for forecasters at National Weather Service Albany to upgrade a prior issued Winter Storm Warning to a Blizzard Warning mere hours prior to snowfall onset in Litchfield County. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 2 AM through nearly 1230 PM Monday, February 23, 2026. Additionally, and unfortunately, there was one recorded death in New Milford in southern Litchfield County. The age and sex of the individual were not available, nor was the location in which they died. However, per the medical examiner's office, the individual died of 'accidental hypothermia' that was likely exacerbated by their prior ailments of dementia and cardiovascular disease. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency, travel ban, road closures, traffic accidents, school closures, power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island. In Connecticut winds were generally lighter and not damaging with snowfall amounts in the 8 to 20 inch range. The highest amounts in Connecticut were in the eastern part of the state. Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 8 to 12 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest reports included 16 inches in Vernon and 15.5 inches in Tolland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of northwest Connecticut from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across northwest Connecticut from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The Governor of Connecticut, Ned Lamont, declared a Winter Storm Emergency on January 25th which ultimately led to a travel ban on commercial vehicles on limited-access highways. During this time, residents were also urged to stay off roads. NWS Albany additionally received reports of numerous school and road closures across northwest Connecticut. ||Key Impacts: Winter Storm Emergency declaration, travel restrictions, school closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 14.7 inches.
